Availability wins

Toronto Tempo 2026 — travel, injuries, and what a performance department can do about it

Author

Hugo Leligny

Published

November 8, 2026

Independent analysis built on public data only (ESPN via SportsDataverse). Not affiliated with the Toronto Tempo or the WNBA. The staff knows things this analysis cannot see (medical information, internal load, game plans): read it as what the public data suggests, and as questions worth discussing, not as answers. Code and pipeline: github.com/hugollel

Summary

The Tempo’s first season ended at 11-33. My starting question was: does travel explain it? Toronto crosses the border far more than any other team, and every West Coast trip ends with a long flight east. To test this, I built a small data platform: a pipeline that loads three seasons of WNBA data into one database, checks the data, and rebuilds who was on the court for every possession. The data pointed somewhere else.

  • Travel costs a little, and the direction of the flight matters. Across the league, teams play slightly below their usual level after flying east (about −2.4 points per 100 possessions after a 3-hour eastward shift). Flying west costs nothing measurable.
  • Injuries decided the season. No team lost more games to injury than Toronto: 111 games missed by rotation players, about 2,800 minutes. The league median is 22.
  • The break is clear. Toronto was 8-8 after 16 games. After Brittney Sykes’ foot injury, it went 3-25.
  • Across the league, availability goes with winning. The champion, Golden State, lost the fewest games to injury (3). Every semifinalist lost 23 games or fewer (league median: 22).
  • Options to discuss: characterise each player’s fatigue, manage minutes and travel with shared reference points, and start the moment players arrive: from Unrivaled, overseas leagues, the NCAA or national teams.

1. Travel: what the schedule really costs

Flying east hurts more than flying west

To measure the cost of travel, I compare each game with what we would expect from that team that night. This part uses all WNBA teams over three seasons (2024–2026), to have enough games: each game counts twice, once for each team (“team-games”).

  • Net rating = points scored minus points allowed, per 100 possessions. In a single game, a positive net rating means the team won.
  • Expected net rating = the team’s level that season − the opponent’s level that season + home court. A statistical model estimates every team’s level season by season, so the Tempo’s level comes from its own 2026 games: no history is needed.
  • Net rating vs expected = actual − expected. Negative means the team played below its usual level that night.

I then average this gap according to the time zone change since the team’s previous game. Only games played within 3 days of the previous one are kept: after a longer break, the team has had time to go home and adjust, so the trip no longer says anything.

The pattern is consistent: the further east a team flies, the more it drops: −0.9, −1.4 and −2.4 points per 100 possessions for 1, 2 and 3 hours. Westward trips show no cost. This matches what we know about the body clock: shifting it earlier (eastward) is harder than shifting it later.

Each point on its own is uncertain (wide intervals). Other schedule factors (back-to-backs, long trips, less rest than the opponent) go in the same direction but are small. Detailed results are in the appendix.

Why it matters for Toronto: the Tempo plays on Eastern time, so every West Coast trip ends with a 3-hour eastward flight home.

Toronto’s road trips, one by one

Each line is one stretch of consecutive games played away from Toronto (including the “home” games moved to Vancouver and Montreal). The bar is the team’s average net rating over those games; the record is wins-losses on the trip; km is the straight-line distance travelled, flight out included; time diff. is the furthest stop’s difference with Toronto.

The two August West Coast swings went 0-5 and 1-5, with 9,179 km and 6,376 km travelled. This is where the season’s worst stretch happened. The next sections show that the main reason was not the travel itself: the roster was also at its thinnest.

2. Injuries: the factor that decided the season

No team lost more to injury

A rotation player is a player averaging 15+ minutes when she plays. I count every game such a player missed through injury or illness (as published by ESPN). Coach’s decisions and national-team absences (for example, players away at the FIBA World Cup in September) are not counted.

  • Toronto lost 111 games of rotation players. Chicago, second, lost 80.
  • Across the 15 teams, games lost to injury and win rate go together (rank correlation −0.57 using minutes lost).
  • The playoffs make it clearer. Golden State won the title with 3 games lost, the fewest in the league. Of the seven teams above the league median, only two made the playoffs. Minnesota finished first in the regular season despite 61 games lost, then went out in the first round.

My reading: a deep roster can survive injuries in the regular season, but deep playoff runs are made by available teams. For an expansion team without depth, keeping players available matters even more.

The season broke when the roster did

The top panel follows the team’s form (5-game average net rating). The bottom panel shows each player, game by game. As the red crosses add up, the line goes down: 8-8 in the first 16 games, 3-25 after. As Laura Juskaite put it: “every game we have a different starting lineup” (TSN).

What changed month by month

Month Record Net rating Rotation players out per game Opponent strength Travel per game
May 5-4 +0.5 1.8 −3.4 1,081 km
June 4-6 −3.2 1.8 −0.8 672 km
July 1-8 −18.2 3.0 +6.3 360 km
August 1-11 −15.1 2.8 +2.4 1,460 km
September 0-4 −24.3 4.0 −1.4 1,257 km

July is the key month. It was the lightest travel month of the season (8 of 9 games as the home team, two of them in Montreal), yet it is when results collapsed. What changed was injuries (from 1.8 to 3 rotation players out) and a tougher set of opponents (+6.3). August then added the heaviest travel on top of a depleted roster.

3. Player by player

Who carried the minutes, who was missing

  • Brittney Sykes (29 min/game) played 17 games. The team was 8-9 with her, 2-24 without her.
  • Kiki Rice missed 15 games mid-season with a grade 2 left ankle sprain, then came back as a starter.
  • Marina Mabrey (hamstring, then right adductor) and Maria Conde / Nyara Sabally (calf) went down in August.
  • Laura Juskaite played all 44 games, and her minutes went up as the injuries piled up: from about 20 in May to about 30 in the final weeks. When absences add up, the load moves to whoever is left. That is how one injury can lead to the next.

On/off: who made the team better on the court?

From the play-by-play I rebuilt the five players on the court for every possession of the season. This lets me compare the team with each player on and off the court.

The team was clearly better with Kiki Rice (+9.5), Isabelle Harrison (+7.4), Julie Allemand (+5.8) and Laura Juskaite (+5.1) on the court. A high scorer does not always lift the team’s net rating (Mabrey: −8.3). One season is a small sample, so I read these numbers as a direction, not a precise value. It still answers a practical question: which players’ availability is worth the most to protect?

Combinations: which duos and trios worked?

Using the same possession-by-possession rebuild, I looked at every group of two or three players who shared the court long enough (150+ minutes for duos, 100+ for trios).

The team averaged −10.7 per 100 possessions over the season. Some groups played clearly above that: Sykes + Sabally + Juskaite (+10.7), and trios built around Fagbenle + Mabrey (+7.5 to +8.2). Others never worked: Fagbenle + Nurse (−41.0) or Fagbenle + Rice + Juskaite (−35.3). The same player can appear in both lists. What counts is the fit between players, and also when they played together: the worst duos played most of their minutes in July and August, when injuries left few options, while Sykes + Sabally played mostly in May. This is a starting point for coaches, not a verdict. With tracking data, the same approach can be applied to who guards whom, spacing and pace.

How players arrived, and what happened

The WNBA has almost no off-season. Many players come into camp straight from another competition. In 2026 the season was also compressed: camp opened April 19, the season started May 8, and the league paused from August 31 to September 16 for the FIBA World Cup in Berlin (Star Tribune).

Player Winter 2025-26 (before camp, April 19) 2026 (as published)
Julie Allemand Fenerbahçe (Turkey): Turkish league and EuroLeague champion, Final Six MVP. The EuroLeague final was on April 19, the day Tempo camp opened (Wikipedia, EuroLeague Women) Hip / thigh, 7 games missed. FIBA World Cup with Belgium in September
Kiki Rice Rookie: NCAA champion with UCLA in April, then draft and camp with no real break Grade 2 left ankle sprain (June 2), 15 games missed (ESPN)
Brittney Sykes Unrivaled, January–March (SI) Plantar fascia issue, then left foot injury (Aug 21), season over, 26 games missed (Just Women’s Sports)
Marina Mabrey Unrivaled, January–March Hamstring, then right adductor in August, season over, 11 games missed
Temi Fagbenle Unrivaled (Lunar Owls); signed with Toronto April 14 (Wikipedia) Absent in two stretches (games 5–12 and 26–30)
Maria Conde Famila Schio (Italy); expansion draft pick April 3, signed April 11 (Wikipedia) Calf, August. FIBA World Cup with Spain in September
Laura Juskaite Žabiny Brno (Czech Republic), EuroLeague from September 2025 (FIBA) All 44 games played, minutes rising from ~20 to ~30
Isabelle Harrison Athletes Unlimited (Nashville, early 2026); signed with Toronto April 12 (Wikipedia) 8 games missed
Kia Nurse Athletes Unlimited (Feb 4 – Mar 1), then Canada’s national team (Mar 11–17); signed with Toronto April 14 (Chicago Sky) 43 of 44 games played
Nyara Sabally Skipped the winter to rest her right knee after a 2025 season limited to 17 games by knee problems (Yahoo Sports) Calf, August; 13 games missed. Knee surgery after the season (EssentiallySports)

Nine of the ten main players went straight from one competition to another: EuroLeague, Unrivaled, Athletes Unlimited, the NCAA or a national team. The only one who rested did so because of a knee problem. Julie Allemand played the EuroLeague final on the day camp opened. The head coach and an assistant also left for the World Cup with their own national teams (TSN). Most of the injuries were lower-limb muscle or tendon problems (calf, hamstring, adductor, foot). These are load-sensitive injuries: the kind a monitoring program is built to anticipate. Rice’s ankle sprain is different: an acute, in-game event.

4. Options to discuss

The public data shows that availability decided the season. It cannot show why a given player broke down, or when the risk was building. That is the job of the club’s own data, and of the staff who know the players. Below are options I would bring to that discussion, not a finished plan.

Start at arrival: know each player’s context

Every player arrives with a different history: an NCAA title run, an Unrivaled winter, a European season, a World Cup ahead. At camp, I would build each player’s baseline:

  • Load history: games and minutes in the last 6–12 months, and when her last real break was
  • Injury history, with the medical staff
  • Baseline tests: weight, CMJ and SJ, grip strength, resting heart rate and HRV, sleep habits

With this baseline, the rest of the season compares each player to herself, not to the team average.

Monitor in three levels

Level What Why
Daily (< 2 min) Morning HRV and resting heart rate, wellness questionnaire (sleep, soreness, stress, mood), weight Autonomic and perceived fatigue, early warning
1–2× per week / pre-game CMJ / SJ (jump height, FT:CT, RSImod), grip strength Neuromuscular fatigue
Every session and game External load from wearables (accelerations, decelerations, jumps), session RPE × duration, nutrition What the body was asked to do, and how hard it felt

One in-game indicator everyone understands

In baseball, bat speed tells you about a hitter’s readiness at a glance. In basketball, my equivalent would be jump height during the game, compared with the player’s own normal level, measured by the wearable sensors (IMU) already used in pro basketball. A second marker: high-intensity changes of direction (accelerations and decelerations) per minute played.

Quarter by quarter. For each player and each quarter, the report would show:

Marker How it is calculated Compared with Flag when
Jump height Average height of her jumps in the quarter (and her best jumps) Her own baseline for that quarter Clear drop, e.g. more than 2 typical errors below
High-intensity changes of direction Number of hard accelerations and decelerations ÷ minutes played in the quarter Her own baseline for that quarter Clear drop over the game, especially Q3–Q4

When is a drop meaningful? Each player gets her own reference, built over several games: her usual value and her usual game-to-game variation (typical error). A change counts as real when it is larger than this normal noise, for example below her smallest worthwhile change or more than 2 typical errors under her baseline. Comparing her with the team average would hide individual profiles.

What a drop can mean:

  • Jump height down, changes of direction stable: first sign of neuromuscular fatigue (legs less reactive, effort still there)
  • Both down, from the 3rd quarter: global fatigue, or a player carrying too many minutes
  • Drop already in Q1: she started the game tired. Check that morning’s HRV, wellness and CMJ, and the last trip
  • Drop the game after a long trip or an eastward flight: travel and sleep, not training load

Caution: a lower average jump height can also come from her role that night (fewer rebounds, more perimeter play). I would compare similar actions (rebounds, contested shots) or use her top jumps of each quarter, and confirm with the next-morning CMJ. The in-game data raises the flag, the morning tests confirm it, and the staff decides.

Characterise the fatigue, then adjust the load

The goal is not only “less load”. It is the right kind of load for the kind of fatigue:

Signal Type of fatigue Possible response
Jump height ↓, FT:CT ↑ Neuromuscular Remove jumps and high-intensity work, keep skill and low-intensity volume
HRV ↓ over several days, resting HR ↑ Autonomic / systemic Protect sleep, low-intensity sessions, review travel and recovery
Wellness ↓ (sleep, stress, mood) Perceived / psychological Talk with the player, adjust the schedule, involve support staff
Soreness ↑ in one area Local / tissue Targeted work with the medical team, adjust exposure

Plan travel, especially flights east

The schedule load index used in this project adds points for back-to-backs, long trips, time-zone shifts, eastward flights, border crossings and dense weeks. It works like a traffic light for each game (Standard / Adjusted / Priority). For Toronto, three ideas are worth testing with the staff:

  1. Consider the return from every West Coast trip as a Priority day. Plan the flight time, light exposure and sleep for the 3-hour eastward shift, and keep the next day light.
  2. On short western trips, consider staying on Toronto time (meals, sleep, training times) instead of adapting to the local time.
  3. Long swings (5–6 games, 6,000–9,000 km) benefit from a plan before departure: where to train, sleep windows, food on the road (customs makes this harder), and load targets per player.

Manage minutes when absences pile up

When injuries pile up, minutes concentrate on the remaining players. That is exactly when the next injury is most likely. One option is to track each player’s minutes like any other load: last 7 days vs her usual level. The data would only flag it; the decision stays with the coaches and the medical staff (cap minutes, change the role, or protect a practice day).

Plugging the club’s data into this platform

The pipeline is built so internal data can join directly. Every table uses the same keys (player and date), so a monitoring table (HRV, CMJ, wellness, wearable load) joins the game, minutes and on/off tables without manual work. The next steps would be:

  • a player_daily_readiness table, with each value compared to the player’s own baseline
  • automatic alerts when a player crosses her thresholds, using the same quality-check approach as the pipeline
  • a simple dashboard for coaches and medical staff: one page per player, with readiness, load and schedule context

5. How it’s built

The analysis sits on a small data platform I built for this project. It uses Python, SQL and DuckDB, and every step can be re-run with one command.

01_ingest.py        download raw data (ESPN via SportsDataverse), log every file
02_load_db.py       load into DuckDB (raw schema), detect schema changes between seasons
03_transform.py     SQL: clean tables (games, teams, player-games) + analysis tables
                    (rest, travel km, time zones, border crossings, rolling 7-day load)
04_quality_checks   14 automatic checks, history kept, pipeline stops on failure
05_analysis.py      schedule effects, time zones, road trips
06_lineups.py       rebuild the 5 players on court from play-by-play, on/off
07_season.py        availability, injuries, player-by-player, playoffs, duos and trios
08_roster.py        four factors, shot zones and shot charts, recruiting profile (part 2)

Data volume: 3 seasons, 927 games, ~17,800 player-games, ~145,000 play-by-play events (2026).

Data quality, checked automatically:

  • Scores match across sources (schedule, team box score, sum of player points): 100%
  • Lineup rebuild: rebuilt minutes within 2 minutes of the official box score for 100% of player-games, and points match the final score for 100% of team-games
  • Schema drift detected: the source added 4 columns in 2026. The pipeline loads all seasons by column name, so nothing breaks.
  • Source lag detected: on November 5, the feed still missed Game 7 of the Finals. The pipeline flags it and uses a documented manual value.

6. Limits

  • Public data shows associations, not causes. I cannot prove why a player got injured.
  • Absence reasons come from ESPN and can be incomplete or vague.
  • One season of one team is a small sample. On/off values and travel effects carry wide uncertainty.
  • Travel distances are straight lines between arenas, not real flight paths.
  • On/off numbers do not separate a player from her teammates and opponents. A next step would be an adjusted plus-minus (a ridge regression on the stints already rebuilt), which estimates each player’s impact while accounting for who else was on the court; it needs more than one season to be stable.
  • Bench players are mostly outside this analysis. On/off and minutes focus on the main rotation, because a player with very few minutes gives numbers that are too noisy. Yet the bench is exactly what plays when injuries hit. A next step would be a dedicated bench analysis: how lineups with two or more bench players performed, how many minutes the bench had to absorb as absences grew, and which bench players held up.
